clinicalPearls: Typical atrial flutter is a macroreentrant right atrial circuit dependent on the cavotricuspid isthmus, producing an atrial rate of approximately 250 to 350 beats per minute.
Counterclockwise typical flutter shows the classic sawtooth negative flutter waves in the inferior leads and positive deflections in V1.
Ventricular response is often regular at a fixed conduction ratio, most commonly 2 to 1, giving a ventricular rate near 150 that should always prompt a search for flutter waves.
Vagal manoeuvres or adenosine transiently increase atrioventricular block and unmask the underlying flutter waves without terminating the arrhythmia.
Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is highly effective and curative for typical isthmus-dependent flutter.
Atypical (non-isthmus-dependent) flutter frequently arises around atrial scar or prior surgical or ablation lesions and requires detailed mapping.
Thromboembolic risk parallels that of atrial fibrillation, so anticoagulation decisions follow the same risk-stratification principles.
One-to-one atrioventricular conduction can occur when a class Ic antiarrhythmic slows the atrial rate without an AV-nodal blocker, dangerously accelerating the ventricular response.
reference.pathophysiology: Atrial flutter is a macroreentrant atrial tachycardia in which a single large reentry circuit sustains rapid, organised atrial activation. In typical flutter the wavefront circulates around the tricuspid annulus within the right atrium, constrained anteriorly by the annulus and posteriorly by the crista terminalis and Eustachian ridge, with the cavotricuspid isthmus forming a critical slow-conduction corridor. The atrioventricular node cannot conduct every rapid atrial impulse, so physiological block produces a slower, frequently regular ventricular response. Atypical flutters use alternative circuits, often around regions of atrial scar, surgical incisions or the mitral annulus, and are common in patients with structural or post-operative atrial disease.
additionalDifferentials: sinus tachycardia with prominent P waves
additionalInvestigations: twelve-lead ECG to identify flutter-wave morphology and conduction ratio
vagal manoeuvre or adenosine to increase block and reveal flutter waves
transthoracic echocardiography to assess chamber size and structural disease
transoesophageal echocardiography before cardioversion when indicated to exclude thrombus
thyroid function tests and electrolytes to identify precipitants
electrophysiological study with entrainment mapping to confirm isthmus dependence
redFlags: one-to-one atrioventricular conduction producing an extremely rapid ventricular rate
haemodynamic instability with hypotension or pulmonary oedema
new flutter in the context of acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism
rapid uncontrolled rates precipitating tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy
flutter with pre-excitation over an accessory pathway
reference.prognosis: With rate or rhythm control, anticoagulation and cavotricuspid isthmus ablation for typical flutter, outcomes are generally good and ablation success rates are high. Persistent rapid rates risk tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy, and many patients subsequently develop atrial fibrillation.
pitfalls: Overlooking flutter in a regular narrow tachycardia at about 150 per minute because alternate flutter waves hide within the QRS and T waves.
Prescribing a class Ic agent without AV-nodal blockade and provoking 1 to 1 conduction.
Neglecting anticoagulation on the mistaken assumption that flutter carries lower thromboembolic risk than fibrillation.
Attributing atypical flutter to a typical isthmus-dependent circuit and targeting the wrong ablation site.
Failing to look for reversible precipitants such as thyrotoxicosis, sepsis or pulmonary disease.
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with supraventricular tachycardia
Zipes Cardiac Electrophysiology: From Cell to Bedside
management: Control the ventricular rate with atrioventricular nodal blocking agents such as beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers where a rate-control strategy is chosen

Restore sinus rhythm by synchronised direct-current cardioversion or pharmacological cardioversion, preceded by transoesophageal echocardiography to exclude atrial thrombus when the patient is not adequately anticoagulated
Provide anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant or warfarin according to thromboembolic risk
Offer cavotricuspid isthmus ablation as the highly effective, curative treatment for typical isthmus-dependent flutter, with detailed mapping and ablation for atypical circuits
Identify and treat precipitants such as thyroid dysfunction and electrolyte disturbance
Monitor for tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy from persistent rapid rates and for subsequent development of atrial fibrillation
